final_proof:
Let \(m\in M\). Since \(M\) is locally Euclidean of dimension \(d\), there are an open neighborhood \(W\) of \(m\), an open set \(O\subseteq\mathbb R^d\), and a homeomorphism \(\varphi:W\to O\). Put \(x=\varphi(m)\). Because \(O\) is open and contains \(x\), there is an \(r>0\) such that the open Euclidean ball \(B(x,r)\) is contained in \(O\).

For each \(n\in\mathbb N\), define
\[
U_n=\varphi^{-1}\!\left(B\left(x,\frac{r}{n+1}\right)\right).
\]
(If \(\mathbb N\) begins at \(1\), one may equivalently use the radii \(r/n\).) Since \(B(x,r/(n+1))\) is open in \(O\) and \(\varphi\) is a homeomorphism, \(U_n\) is open in \(W\). Because \(W\) is open in \(M\), \(U_n\) is open in \(M\), and it contains \(m\). Moreover, the restriction
\[
\varphi^{-1}\big|_{B(x,r/(n+1))}:B\left(x,\frac{r}{n+1}\right)\longrightarrow U_n
\]
is a homeomorphism. Thus every \(U_n\) is the homeomorphic image of an open ball in \(\mathbb R^d\).

It remains to verify the local-basis property. Let \(V\) be any neighborhood of \(m\) in \(M\). There is an open set \(G\subseteq M\) such that \(m\in G\subseteq V\). The set \(G\cap W\) is open in \(W\) and contains \(m\), so \(\varphi(G\cap W)\) is an open subset of \(O\) containing \(x\). Since \(O\) is open in \(\mathbb R^d\), this is also open in \(\mathbb R^d\). Hence there is some \(\varepsilon>0\) such that
\[
B(x,\varepsilon)\subseteq\varphi(G\cap W).
\]
By the Archimedean property, choose \(n\in\mathbb N\) such that \(r/(n+1)<\varepsilon\). Then
\[
U_n=\varphi^{-1}\!\left(B\left(x,\frac{r}{n+1}\right)\right)
\subseteq G\cap W\subseteq V.
\]
Thus every neighborhood of \(m\) contains some \(U_n\). Therefore \((U_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}\) is a countable local basis at \(m\), and each of its members is the homeomorphic image of an open ball in \(\mathbb R^d\), as claimed.
